question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

SALUBRIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Wholesome.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Salubrious (adjective) means health-giving; favourable to health and well-being. It is used above all of climate, air and surroundings. (स्वास्थ्यप्रद, हितकर)
◦ Example: The family moved to the hills for the more salubrious climate.

 

• Wholesome carries the same sense — conducive to good health of body or mind. (स्वास्थ्यवर्धक)
◦ Example: The hostel now serves simple, wholesome food.

 

• The word comes from Latin salus (health, safety) — the same root as salutary (producing a beneficial effect) and salutation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Unwholesome (अस्वास्थ्यकर): harmful to health — the direct opposite of salubrious.

 

• Option 2: Injurious (हानिकारक): causing harm or damage — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Toxic (विषाक्त): poisonous — again an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the arrangement: three antonyms and one synonym. Fix the meaning of the given word first, then discard every option that agrees with the majority sense.

 

• Other synonyms of salubrious: healthful, salutary, bracing, invigorating, sanitary. Antonyms: insalubrious, noxious, deleterious, pernicious.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

NADIR
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Zenith.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nadir (noun) means the lowest point — the moment of greatest depression or misfortune in someone's affairs. (निम्नतम बिंदु)
◦ Example: The party reached its nadir after losing every seat in the state.

 

• Its true opposite is zenith — the highest point; the peak of success or power. (शिखर, पराकाष्ठा)
◦ Example: The empire was at its zenith under his grandson.

 

• Both are astronomical terms: the zenith is the point of the sky directly overhead and the nadir the point directly beneath one's feet. They are exact opposites by definition, which is why SSC pairs them so often.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Bottom (तल): the lowest part of something — a synonym in sense.

 

• Option 3: Depth (गहराई): the state of being deep, or the lowest reach — also close in sense to nadir.

 

• Option 4: Trough (गर्त): the low point of a wave or of an economic cycle — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of nadir: apex, pinnacle, summit, acme, apogee, climax.

 

• Useful astronomical pair to remember alongside it: perigee (nearest point to the earth) and apogee (farthest point).

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To turn the tables
option_1: To reverse a situation so that it now favours oneself
option_2: To rearrange the furniture of a room hastily
option_3: To postpone an awkward decision indefinitely
option_4: To share the credit for a success equally
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To reverse a situation so that it now favours oneself.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "To turn the tables" means to reverse one's position relative to an opponent, so that the person previously at a disadvantage gains the upper hand. (पासा पलट देना)
◦ Example: Trailing by two sets, she turned the tables in the third and won the match.

 

• The expression comes from board games such as chess and backgammon, in which players once literally turned the board round so that each took over the other's position.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes the idiom literally, which is the standard trap in idiom questions.

 

• Option 3 describes delay, for which the idiom would be "to put something on the back burner" or "to kick the can down the road".

 

• Option 4 describes shared credit, nearer to "to go halves".

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of reversal: "The boot is on the other foot", "The tables have turned", "To beat someone at their own game" and "To give someone a taste of their own medicine".

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

MENDACITY
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Veracity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mendacity (noun) means untruthfulness; the habit of telling lies. (मिथ्यावादिता, झूठ)
◦ Example: The inquiry exposed the mendacity of the entire submission.

 

• Its true opposite is veracity — habitual truthfulness; conformity to the facts. (सत्यनिष्ठा)
◦ Example: No one has ever questioned the veracity of her accounts.

 

• The roots make the pair easy to hold: Latin mendax (lying) against verax (truthful), the latter also giving verify, verdict and veritable.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Falsehood (असत्य): an untrue statement, or untruthfulness in general — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Duplicity (कपट): deceitfulness, especially saying one thing while intending another — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Prevarication (टालमटोल, बहानेबाजी): evasive or misleading speech intended to avoid the truth — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of mendacity: candour, honesty, probity, rectitude, frankness.

 

• Do not confuse mendacity (lying) with mendicancy (begging) — a pair SSC has set against each other more than once.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the process in which nutrient enrichment of a water body causes excessive growth of algae.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Eutrophication.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Eutrophication" is the enrichment of a lake, pond or river with nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates, usually from fertiliser run-off or sewage, which triggers dense algal growth and, as the algae decay, a fall in dissolved oxygen that kills fish. (सुपोषण)
◦ Example: Fertiliser run-off from the surrounding fields has caused severe eutrophication of the lake.

 

• Break the word into its Greek roots: EU (well, good) + TROPHE (nourishment) + -ATION (process). The same roots appear in eulogy, euphony and atrophy (wasting away for want of nourishment).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Eutropication" — incorrect; the "h" of trophe has been dropped.

 

• Option 2: "Utrophication" — incorrect; the prefix is "eu", not "u".

 

• Option 3: "Eutrophycation" — incorrect; the suffix is "-ication", with an i, not a y.

 

NOTE

 

• Related environmental terms worth remembering: biomagnification (build-up of toxins up a food chain), bioremediation (use of organisms to clean pollution), desalination (removal of salt from water) and biochemical oxygen demand (BOD).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A specialist who identifies, names and classifies living organisms'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Taxonomist.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A taxonomist is a scientist who works in taxonomy — the branch of biology concerned with naming, describing and classifying organisms into groups such as kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. (वर्गिकीविद)
◦ Example: The taxonomist confirmed that the specimen belonged to a previously undescribed genus.

 

• The word comes from Greek taxis (arrangement, order) + nomos (law) — literally the law of arrangement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Taxidermist (पशु-त्वचा भरने वाला): one who stuffs and mounts the skins of dead animals for display. The similarity of spelling makes this the intended trap.

 

• Option 3: Ecologist (पारिस्थितिकीविद): one who studies the relations of organisms to one another and to their surroundings.

 

• Option 4: Anatomist (शारीर रचना विशेषज्ञ): one who studies the internal structure of organisms.

 

NOTE

 

• Other specialist one-word substitutes tested by SSC: Ornithologist (birds), Entomologist (insects), Ichthyologist (fishes), Herpetologist (reptiles), Palaeontologist (fossils), Epigraphist (inscriptions) and Numismatist (coins).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The number of applicants ___ risen sharply since the examination fee was waived.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. has.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The rule turns on the article:

◦ "The number of" + plural noun → SINGULAR verb. The subject is the number itself, a single figure.
◦ "A number of" + plural noun → PLURAL verb. Here a number of simply means many, and the plural noun is the real subject.

 

• Since the sentence uses "The number of applicants", the singular "has" is required.

◦ Correct: The number of applicants has risen sharply.
◦ Compare: A number of applicants have withdrawn their forms.

 

• The past participle "risen" also confirms that a perfect tense is needed, which rules out were and are.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: have — wrongly treats applicants as the subject.

 

• Options 2 and 4: were / are — forms of be, which cannot combine with risen to form a correct tense.

 

NOTE

 

• The same distinction applies to "the majority of", "a variety of" and "a total of". Note also that rise is intransitive (prices rise) while raise is transitive (they raised the fee), so risen never takes a passive form.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The proposed amendments militate ___ the interests of small traders in the border districts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. against.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Militate against" means to be a powerful factor working to prevent or oppose something. The verb is almost always used with "against" and takes an abstract object such as interests, success, chances or a proposal. (विरुद्ध जाना, बाधक होना)
◦ Example: His frequent absences militated against his promotion.

 

• The verb comes from Latin miles, militis (a soldier) — the same root as military and militant, which is why the sense is one of active opposition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: for — would reverse the meaning; militate has no positive use.

 

• Option 3: with — belongs with the different verb "mitigate", which is not followed by with either.

 

• Option 4: upon — not used with this verb.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not confuse militate against (to work against) with mitigate (to make less severe). Mitigate takes a direct object: steps were taken to mitigate the damage. Writing mitigate against is a common error.

 

• Other verbs fixed with against: discriminate against, guard against, caution against, decide against and weigh against.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

If the file ___ been submitted on time, the sanction would have come through before the audit.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. had.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The main clause reads "would have come through", which identifies the sentence as a Third Conditional — used for an unreal situation in the past, one that did not in fact happen.

 

• The fixed structure is: If + subject + had + V3, … would have + V3.

◦ Correct: If the file had been submitted on time, the sanction would have come through.
◦ Example: If she had studied the notification, she would have applied in time.

 

• The essential rule: "would" never appears in the if-clause. It belongs only in the main clause.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: has — the present perfect cannot be used in a third conditional.

 

• Option 2: would have — places would inside the if-clause, the commonest error in conditionals.

 

• Option 3: have — disagrees with the singular subject the file and gives the wrong tense.

 

NOTE

 

• The three conditionals:
◦ First (real future): If it rains, we will cancel the trip.
◦ Second (unreal present): If I knew the answer, I would tell you.
◦ Third (unreal past): If I had known, I would have told you.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The Principal, as well as the senior teachers, (1)/ were present at the function (2)/ organised in the school auditorium (3)/ to felicitate the retiring librarian. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase "as well as the senior teachers" is a parenthetical addition, not part of the subject. The real subject remains "The Principal", which is singular, so the verb must be "was".

◦ Corrected sentence: The Principal, as well as the senior teachers, was present at the function organised in the school auditorium to felicitate the retiring librarian.

 

• The pair of commas around the phrase is itself the clue: whatever stands between them can be lifted out without damaging the sentence, and the verb must agree with what is left.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the phrase is properly enclosed within a pair of commas.

 

• Part (3) is correct — organised in is the right form of the past-participle phrase.

 

• Part (4) is correct — the infinitive of purpose to felicitate is well formed.

 

NOTE

 

• Expressions that do not change the number of the subject: as well as, along with, together with, in addition to, accompanied by, besides, including, no less than and rather than.
◦ The captain, along with his players, was felicitated.
◦ But with "and" the subject really is plural: The captain and his players were felicitated.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The candidates which had applied (1)/ well before the last date (2)/ were called for document verification (3)/ at the regional office. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The relative pronoun "which" is used for animals and things, never for persons. Since the antecedent here is "the candidates", the correct pronoun is "who" (or that).

◦ Corrected sentence: The candidates who had applied well before the last date were called for document verification at the regional office.

 

• The complete rule: who for persons, which for animals and things, that for either, and whose for possession with both.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct — before the last date is a well-formed adverbial of time.

 

• Part (3) is correct — the plural subject candidates agrees with the plural verb were called.

 

• Part (4) is correct — at is the right preposition before the name of an office.

 

NOTE

 

• Points on relative pronouns regularly tested by SSC:
◦ After a superlative, and after all, any, none, only, same and nothing, use that: This is the best film that I have seen.
◦ That can never follow a preposition or a comma: the office in which he works, not in that.
◦ Use whom as the object: the officer whom we met.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

Can the department revise the seniority list before December?
option_1: Can the department be revised the seniority list before December?
option_2: Can the seniority list revised by the department before December?
option_3: Can the seniority list be revised by the department before December?
option_4: Can the seniority list being revised by the department before December?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Can the seniority list be revised by the department before December?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is a Yes/No interrogative containing a modal. In the passive, a modal question follows the pattern: Modal + object + be + V3 + by + subject?

◦ Active: Can the department revise the seniority list?
◦ Passive: Can the seniority list be revised by the department?

 

• The modal itself — "can" — stays at the front of the sentence and never changes form, and the question mark is retained.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the department as the subject, so it reads as though the department were being revised.

 

• Option 2 omits "be", which is essential after a modal in the passive.

 

• Option 4 uses "being revised", a continuous form that cannot follow a modal in this structure.

 

NOTE

 

• Passive patterns for questions: Do/Does + V1 → am/is/are + V3; Did + V1 → was/were + V3; Modal + V1 → modal + be + V3; Has/Have + V3 → has/have been + V3. A Wh- question keeps its question word at the front: Why can the list not be revised?

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The revised guidelines have been circulated to all branches by the head office.
option_1: The head office has circulated the revised guidelines to all branches.
option_2: The head office had circulated the revised guidelines to all branches.
option_3: The head office circulated the revised guidelines to all branches.
option_4: The head office is circulating the revised guidelines to all branches.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The head office has circulated the revised guidelines to all branches.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Present Perfect Passive — structure: has/have been + V3. Its active counterpart is the Present Perfect Active — has/have + V3.

◦ Passive: The revised guidelines have been circulated by the head office.
◦ Active: The head office has circulated the revised guidelines.

 

• Note that the auxiliary changes from "have" to "has", because it must now agree with the new subject, the head office, which is singular. Agreement always follows the subject of the sentence you are writing, not the one you started from.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses the past perfect, which pushes the action further back than the original.

 

• Option 3 uses the simple past, losing the present perfect's link with the present.

 

• Option 4 uses the present continuous, making the action ongoing rather than completed.

 

NOTE

 

• A useful check in every voice conversion: after rewriting, ask whether the auxiliary agrees with the new subject and whether the tense is unchanged. Most wrong options in SSC alter exactly one of these two things.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The department invited an eminent economist to deliver the annual lecture.
option_1: The eminent scholar chaired the closing session.
option_2: An eminent lawyer argued the case before the bench.
option_3: She is an eminent authority on medieval inscriptions.
option_4: The heavy clouds suggested that rain was imminent.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The heavy clouds suggested that rain was imminent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and has a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Eminent means distinguished, respected and well known in a profession. It describes people.
• Imminent means about to happen very soon. It describes events. The two are pronounced almost identically, so "imminent" is the homophone required.

◦ Example: The collapse of the old bridge appeared imminent.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 all reuse the same spelling "eminent" in the sense of distinguished, so none of them supplies a homophone.

 

NOTE

 

• Memory aid: eminent people excel; an imminent event is immediate.

 

• A third member of the same family is worth knowing: immanent, meaning inherent or existing within, as in an immanent quality of the system.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

When India began replacing its old weights and measures with the metric system in the late 1950s, the change was widely expected to fail. The country had used seers, maunds and tolas along with a dozen regional variants of each, and the same word often stood for different quantities in adjacent districts. Traders had every reason to prefer the confusion, since a buyer who could not verify a measure could not dispute a price.

 

The reform was therefore designed as much around habit as around arithmetic. Instead of announcing a single changeover date, the government moved commodity by commodity and region by region across nearly a decade, so that a shopkeeper had to learn one new unit at a time. School textbooks were revised ahead of the market, on the reasoning that children would carry the new units home. Inspectors were supplied with standard weights to lend and not merely to seize, which turned an enforcement exercise into a supply one.

 

Resistance was real but narrower than predicted. It came less from consumers, who gained from a measure that meant the same everywhere, than from intermediaries whose margins depended on ambiguity. That the reform eventually succeeded is now cited as evidence that Indians accept rational systems readily. The inference is too generous. What the episode actually shows is that a reform survives when the cost of complying with it is deliberately kept lower than the cost of resisting it.

 

The lesson has been forgotten more often than it has been applied. Later attempts at standardisation — of building codes, of land records, of school-leaving certificates — have generally been announced as deadlines rather than designed as transitions, and have taken far longer to accomplish a good deal less.

 

According to the passage, why did traders prefer the old system of weights and measures?
option_1: Because the old units were easier for illiterate people to remember
option_2: Because a buyer unable to verify a measure could not dispute the price
option_3: Because the metric system required expensive new equipment
option_4: Because regional units carried greater cultural prestige
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Because a buyer unable to verify a measure could not dispute the price.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first paragraph states it directly: traders had every reason to prefer the confusion, since a buyer who could not verify a measure could not dispute a price.

 

• The confusion was real and useful — the same word stood for different quantities in adjacent districts, so no buyer could carry a fixed standard from one market to the next. The advantage lay entirely with the seller.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 invents a reason about memory and literacy that the passage never gives.

 

• Option 2 is the only option grounded in the text; the others are plausible-sounding but absent.

 

• Options 3 and 4 raise cost and cultural prestige, neither of which is discussed anywhere in the passage.

 

NOTE

 

• For questions beginning "why", look for the connectives since, because, as or for. Here the word "since" marks the answer in the very sentence that raises the point.

Which of the following was NOT part of the strategy adopted for the changeover?
option_1: Moving commodity by commodity and region by region over nearly a decade
option_2: Revising school textbooks ahead of the market
option_3: Announcing a single nationwide changeover date
option_4: Giving inspectors standard weights to lend rather than only to seize
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Announcing a single nationwide changeover date.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The second paragraph states the opposite: instead of announcing a single changeover date, the government moved commodity by commodity and region by region across nearly a decade.

 

• The other three options are all named in that paragraph as deliberate features of the design — gradual sequencing, textbooks revised ahead of the market so that children would carry the new units home, and inspectors supplied with weights to lend and not merely to seize, which turned enforcement into supply.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are each stated almost word for word in the passage and are therefore wrong answers to a NOT question.

 

• The final paragraph confirms the point from the other direction: later reforms failed precisely because they were announced as deadlines rather than designed as transitions.

 

NOTE

 

• In "which … NOT" questions, three options will be traceable to the passage and one will not. Mark each option against the text before choosing, and beware of selecting a correct statement out of habit.

From whom, according to the passage, did the resistance chiefly come?
option_1: From consumers unwilling to learn new units
option_2: From schoolteachers asked to revise their syllabus
option_3: From inspectors reluctant to enforce the new rules
option_4: From intermediaries whose margins depended on ambiguity
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. From intermediaries whose margins depended on ambiguity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The third paragraph is explicit: resistance came less from consumers, who gained from a measure that meant the same everywhere, than from intermediaries whose margins depended on ambiguity.

 

• The distinction matters to the author's argument. Because the losers were a narrow group and the gainers a broad one, the reform could be pushed through — resistance was real but narrower than predicted.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the passage — consumers are named as the gainers.

 

• Options 2 and 3 name groups that appear in the passage only as instruments of the reform, never as opponents of it.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch the construction "less from X than from Y". It is a comparison, not a denial, and the answer is always Y. SSC reliably builds a distractor out of X.

Which of the following best captures the core theme of the passage?
option_1: A reform survives when complying with it is made cheaper than resisting it
option_2: Indians accept rational systems more readily than other peoples do
option_3: The metric system is arithmetically superior to traditional units
option_4: Enforcement is the most effective instrument of administrative reform
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A reform survives when complying with it is made cheaper than resisting it.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The author states the thesis in as many words: what the episode actually shows is that a reform survives when the cost of complying with it is deliberately kept lower than the cost of resisting it.

 

• Everything else in the passage supports that claim — the gradual sequencing, the textbooks, the lent weights, and the closing contrast with later reforms announced as deadlines rather than designed as transitions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 is the inference the author expressly rejects, calling it too generous.

 

• Option 3 takes up the arithmetic, which the author sets aside in favour of habit.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the passage, which praises the shift away from pure enforcement towards supply.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage contains the words "what this actually shows", "the point is" or "in essence", the sentence that follows is almost always the thesis, and the central-theme question is built on it.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

When India began replacing its old weights and measures with the metric system in the late 1950s, the change was widely expected to fail. The country had used seers, maunds and tolas along with a dozen regional variants of each, and the same word often stood for different quantities in adjacent districts. Traders had every reason to prefer the confusion, since a buyer who could not verify a measure could not dispute a price.

 

The reform was therefore designed as much around habit as around arithmetic. Instead of announcing a single changeover date, the government moved commodity by commodity and region by region across nearly a decade, so that a shopkeeper had to learn one new unit at a time. School textbooks were revised ahead of the market, on the reasoning that children would carry the new units home. Inspectors were supplied with standard weights to lend and not merely to seize, which turned an enforcement exercise into a supply one.

 

Resistance was real but narrower than predicted. It came less from consumers, who gained from a measure that meant the same everywhere, than from intermediaries whose margins depended on ambiguity. That the reform eventually succeeded is now cited as evidence that Indians accept rational systems readily. The inference is too generous. What the episode actually shows is that a reform survives when the cost of complying with it is deliberately kept lower than the cost of resisting it.

 

The lesson has been forgotten more often than it has been applied. Later attempts at standardisation — of building codes, of land records, of school-leaving certificates — have generally been announced as deadlines rather than designed as transitions, and have taken far longer to accomplish a good deal less.

 

What is the author's tone in discussing later attempts at standardisation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Analytical and mildly critical.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The closing paragraph observes that the lesson has been forgotten more often than it has been applied, and that later reforms have taken far longer to accomplish a good deal less. That is plainly a criticism.

 

• The criticism is nevertheless measured. The author names no culprit, uses no abusive language, and offers a reason for the failure — that these reforms were announced as deadlines rather than designed as transitions. Judgement supported by analysis, expressed without heat, is exactly what analytical and mildly critical describes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the sense; there is nothing admiring about the closing lines.

 

• Option 3 overstates the temperature — bitter and dismissive would require anger or contempt, which the restrained phrasing avoids.

 

• Option 4 ignores the clear evaluative language (forgotten, far longer, a good deal less), which shows the author is not merely describing.

 

NOTE

 

• Tone questions usually turn on degree, not direction. Once you have decided that the author is critical, the real choice is between mildly critical and severely critical, and the deciding evidence is the strength of the adjectives used.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

He found it difficult to cope up with the demands of the new syllabus.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. cope with.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "cope" is followed directly by "with". The word "up" is superfluous, and "cope up with", though extremely common in Indian usage, is not standard English.

◦ Corrected sentence: He found it difficult to cope with the demands of the new syllabus.
◦ Example: The hospital struggled to cope with the sudden rush of patients.

 

• The confusion arises from "catch up with" and "keep up with", which do take up. Cope does not.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the original error.

 

• Option 3: "cope up for" compounds the error with a wrong preposition.

 

• Option 4: "coping up with" keeps the superfluous up, and the gerund does not fit after to here.

 

NOTE

 

• Other superfluous-particle errors regularly tested by SSC: discuss (not discuss about), emphasise (not emphasise on), order (not order for), investigate (not investigate into), resemble (not resemble to) and reach (not reach at).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Her elder sister got married with a doctor from Nagpur last winter.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. married to a doctor.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The fixed preposition after "married" is "to", never with.

◦ Corrected sentence: Her elder sister got married to a doctor from Nagpur last winter.
◦ Example: He has been married to her for eleven years.

 

• Note the two correct patterns: "marry somebody" takes no preposition at all (she married a doctor), while "be/get married" takes to (she got married to a doctor). The error arises from translating directly from Hindi, where the equivalent postposition suggests with.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the original error.

 

• Option 2: "married by a doctor" changes the meaning altogether — by would name the person performing the ceremony.

 

• Option 4: "marrying with a doctor" keeps the wrong preposition and uses a form that cannot follow got.

 

NOTE

 

• Other fixed adjective–preposition pairs tested by SSC: acquainted with, angry with (a person) but angry at (a thing), afraid of, ashamed of, jealous of, indifferent to, senior to, popular with and surprised at.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said to her, "Did you attend the departmental meeting?"
option_1: He asked her did she attend the departmental meeting.
option_2: He asked her whether she had attended the departmental meeting.
option_3: He asked her whether she attended the departmental meeting.
option_4: He asked her that whether she had attended the departmental meeting.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He asked her whether she had attended the departmental meeting.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported sentence is a Yes/No question. Its rules of conversion are:

◦ The reporting verb said to becomes asked / enquired of.
◦ The conjunction "if" or "whether" is introduced, since there is no question word to serve as the link.
◦ The question order is dropped — the auxiliary did disappears and the clause takes normal statement order.
◦ The tense is backshifted: did attend → had attended.
◦ The question mark is replaced by a full stop.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 retains the interrogative order (did she attend), which indirect speech does not permit.

 

• Option 3 drops the auxiliary correctly but fails to backshift — the simple past should become the past perfect after asked.

 

• Option 4 uses "that" together with "whether". Only one conjunction may be used; combining them is always wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• "Whether" is preferred to if when the sentence offers alternatives (whether to accept or refuse) and after a preposition (the question of whether…). In simple reporting, either is acceptable.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

The guard warned the children not to lean out of the window.
option_1: "Do not lean out of the window," the guard warned the children.
option_2: "You should not lean out of the window," the guard warned the children.
option_3: "Did you lean out of the window?" the guard asked the children.
option_4: "They must not lean out of the window," the guard warned.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. "Do not lean out of the window," the guard warned the children.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb "warned … not to" is the standard indirect form of a negative imperative. Restoring the direct speech reverses the rules:

◦ "not to + V1" → "Do not + V1", the negative imperative form.
◦ The words are enclosed in inverted commas, and the reporting verb warned is retained since it names the manner of speaking.
◦ The children are addressed directly, so no third-person pronoun appears inside the quotation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses "should not", which gives advice; its indirect form would be advised the children that they should not…

 

• Option 3 turns the warning into a question about a past act, changing the meaning entirely.

 

• Option 4 keeps the third person "they" inside the quotation, so the guard is no longer speaking to the children at all.

 

NOTE

 

• Negative imperatives in narration: "Don't touch the wires," he said → He warned/told them not to touch the wires, or He forbade them to touch the wires. Note that forbid is followed by to, not by not to.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. Kamla had been saving seed from her own fields for as long as anyone in Baghpura could remember.

 

A. Neighbours who had long since switched to bought seed began knocking at her door in the drought year.

 

B. She kept each variety in a separate earthen pot, labelled with a scrap of coloured cloth.

 

C. Only her varieties, bred over decades in that exact soil, had come through the failed rains.

 

D. Within three seasons the pots along her wall had multiplied from nine to over forty.

 

S2. Baghpura now runs a seed bank of its own, and Kamla is paid a small honorarium to look after it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B-A-C-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – C – D – S2. The paragraph follows a practice → event → explanation → consequence order.

 

• S1 describes the practice — Kamla's long habit of saving seed.

◦ B elaborates that practice, telling us how she stored the seed. It belongs immediately after S1 because it says nothing new about events.
◦ A introduces the event — the drought year and the neighbours at her door.
◦ C must follow A, since it explains why they came: only her varieties had survived the failed rains.
◦ D gives the consequence — the pots multiplying — and the words the pots point back to B, rounding the paragraph off before S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-B-C-D) interrupts the drought narrative with a description of storage, so C no longer explains A.

 

• Option 3 (B-C-A-D) gives the explanation before the event it explains.

 

• Option 4 (A-C-B-D) places the storage detail after the crisis, where it has no bearing.

 

NOTE

 

• A reliable principle in narrative rearrangement: description settles before action begins. Sentences that merely elaborate the opening situation come first; sentences that move the story forward follow.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The lightness of a loaf of bread is the work of a single-celled fungus.

 

A. Yeast feeds on the sugars present in the flour and releases carbon dioxide as a by-product.

 

B. The gluten network built up during kneading traps these bubbles instead of letting them escape.

 

C. Baking finally sets the structure in place and drives off the alcohol produced alongside the gas.

 

D. As the dough warms, the trapped gas expands and the loaf visibly swells.

 

S2. What went into the oven as a paste of flour and water comes out as a stable, airy solid.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A-B-D-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – B – D – C – S2. The paragraph describes a process, and process paragraphs always run in the order in which the stages occur.

 

• S1 names the agent — a single-celled fungus.

◦ A identifies it as yeast and states what it does: releasing carbon dioxide. It must come first, since every later sentence depends on there being gas.
◦ B follows A because "these bubbles" can only refer to the carbon dioxide just mentioned.
◦ D follows B, as "the trapped gas" refers to gas already trapped by the gluten network.
◦ C is the final stage — baking sets the structure — and leads directly into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (B-A-D-C) opens with "these bubbles" before any gas has been mentioned.

 

• Option 3 (A-D-B-C) speaks of "the trapped gas" before anything has trapped it.

 

• Option 4 (B-D-A-C) repeats both faults at once.

 

NOTE

 

• In a process paragraph the output of one stage becomes the subject of the next — here carbon dioxide → these bubbles → the trapped gas. Tracing that chain fixes the whole order without any need to understand the science.
